title: Argan / Argosy Gaming / Allergy Therapeutics / Agilysys / Accretive Health — Backlog Quality, Catalyst Path and Governance V9

notes: Raw Short -> actual Long corrections: Argan 2019, Argosy Gaming 2002 and Agilysys 2013.
AGX changes historical identity at the Batch 74/75 boundary: AGX 2000 was Agribrands International, while AGX 2013 onward in this batch is Argan Inc.
No usable source-DB performance rows were found for any of the ten Batch 75 ideas.
Argan 2013 and 2016 succeeded because project financing and full notices to proceed converted headline backlog into revenue and cash quickly.
Argan 2019 failed on the stated FY2021-2023 revenue/EPS horizon because multiple projects remained subject to financing and start-date delays.
Argosy Gaming was acquired by Penn National for $47 cash/share in 2004.
Allergy Therapeutics' 2007 U.S. clinical program was placed on FDA hold; the hold was not lifted until 2012, invalidating the near-term U.S. commercialization path.
Agilysys 2007 is a capital-allocation failure after a large asset sale; 2013 and 2016 correctly identified hospitality-software quality but overestimated near-term sale probability.
Accretive Health's Minnesota legal issue was not existential, but later accounting restatements and delayed filings caused NYSE delisting and invalidated the original public-equity path.
Later strategic or business validation is not backfilled as original-horizon success when the security path was materially impaired.

batch_lessons: EPC backlog should be probability-weighted for financing, full notice to proceed and project schedule rather than treated as booked revenue.
A correct operating forecast can still miss its investment horizon if the catalyst clock is too aggressive.
Historical ticker reuse requires date-specific legal-entity verification; AGX 2000 and AGX 2013+ are different companies.
Core-business value is not a biotech equity floor when that core business must finance the pipeline burn.
Cash-rich rollups must be underwritten through management capital-allocation skill, not cash balance alone.
Activist ownership increases strategic optionality but does not guarantee a company sale.
SOTP value and the path by which that value is realized are separate hypotheses.
A near-term event thesis can fail even if the long-run business-quality thesis ultimately proves excellent.
Controversy investing should search for second-order accounting, governance and control risks beyond the visible headline.
Later strategic validation does not retroactively rescue an original-horizon security thesis that suffered delisting, dilution or other path impairment.
